title: Beyond Family Labels: A Taxonomic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Prior for Avian 3D Shape Recovery
claim: Binary same-group labels keep one bit of hierarchical structure; using every rank of the hierarchy gives graded, continuous similarity.
layout: single panel, top-down tree over species thumbnails, dashed threshold line
description: A single horizontal dendrogram of 17 bird species. Small circular photo thumbnails of birds (Bunting, Cardinal, Crow, Blue Jay, Flycatcher, Grackle, Grosbeak, Waxwing, Flicker, Woodpecker, two Kingfishers, Gull, Puffin, Mallard, Roadrunner, Albatross) sit along the bottom with rotated labels. Tree branches rise above them, colored by order: dark blue for the large songbird group, lighter blues for the woodpecker/kingfisher and gull/puffin groups, and brown, purple and orange for the singleton orders. Left-hand row labels read 'same family', 'same order' and 'sister orders' to mark the rank at which lineages join. A dashed dark-red horizontal line cuts the tree just above the family level. It marks the single bit that the family-contrastive baseline keeps. The eye goes first to the colored tree and the dashed line.
caption: Beyond family labels. The $17$ training species of CtrlAVES3D on the Linnaean tree [ref], colored by order. The height at which two lineages join marks their lowest shared rank, from same family up to outgroup; each rank sets the distance $d_{\mathrm{tax}}$ that our prior reads ([ref]b). The family-supervised contrastive loss of AniMer+ [ref] keeps a single bit of this tree: whether a pair joins below the dashed red line. Our Ornstein--Uhlenbeck (OU) prior uses every rank, pulling the shape codes of two species together more strongly the more closely they are related, so the shape space carries graded structure rather than a same-family indicator.
abstract: Recovering 3D pose and shape of birds from single images is bottlenecked by the long tail of avian diversity: out of ~10,000 species, only a few dozen have 3D-labeled training data, and in-the-wild test sets routinely contain species never seen at training. Generalizing across clades is therefore a central problem. The current state of the art, AniMer+, mitigates it with a family-level contrastive loss that conveys only a binary same-family indicator per pair and discards the continuous structure of the species tree. We propose a taxonomic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck prior on the shape code of the AVES parametric bird mesh model: a multivariate Gaussian whose covariance decays exponentially with Linnaean rank distance, with a learnable selection strength and noise scale. The prior generalizes family contrastive into a continuous, generative form, exposing the graded cross- and within-family similarity that a binary indicator cannot, and brings continuous comparative phylogenetics in as a biology-grounded inductive bias for the long tail. Our method improves over AniMer+ on both metrics of the unseen-species CowBird benchmark and on CtrlAVES3D, while remaining comparable on seen-species CUB. A permutation ablation isolates taxonomic structure from generic Gaussian smoothing, and a rank-granularity ablation identifies cross-order distinctions (the structure beyond a family-vs-not indicator) as the dominant source of the unseen-species gain.
